CausalChain: In HCC, increased extracellular matrix stiffness activates integrin‐β5 on Kupffer cells and infiltrating monocytes → this activation triggers FAK, leading to downstream MEK/ERK signaling and stabilization of HIF1α → these signals drive TAM polarization to an M2 phenotype that secretes immunosuppressive cytokines and supports tumor progression → Dampening ECM stiffness signaling or interrupting integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK cascade may induce repolarization toward the M1 phenotype → M1 TAMs enhance cytotoxic T cell infiltration and anti‐tumor responses.
Hypothesis: Targeting the biophysical properties of the hepatic tumor microenvironment by modulating ECM stiffness or interrupting integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling can reprogram tumor‐associated macrophages from an immunosuppressive M2 type to an immunostimulatory M1 type, thereby enhancing anti‐tumor immunity and increasing the efficacy of HCC immunotherapies.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is distinguished by a complex tumor microenvironment in which physiological and molecular cues converge to modulate the phenotype of tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs). Recent studies have implicated not only cytokine secretions and metabolic reprogramming but also biophysical factors—namely, the altered stiffness of the extracellular matrix—in directing TAM polarization toward an immunosuppressive, pro‐tumoral (M2) phenotype. Here we propose a novel hypothesis that by modulating matrix stiffness‐mediated signaling, particularly via the integrin‐β5/FAK/MEK/ERK cascade, one can redirect TAM differentiation toward a pro‐inflammatory (M1) state. Such reprogramming would restore effective anti‐tumor immunity and improve responses to immunotherapy in HCC.
